subject: ventures/landscape-lighting-bid-calculator
professional: a low-voltage landscape lighting contractor who designs and bids residential systems; first checks: is the transformer sized to the connected load at about 80% of its rating (VA, not just LED watts), does the wire gauge and run length keep voltage drop on the 12 V runs within about 10% (VD = 2 x length x ohms/ft x amps), are hub/T-method versus daisy-chain layouts and multi-tap transformers reflected, does a fixtures-only job really carry no trench or transformer, and is the price built as margin on price rather than markup on cost

evidence.correctness: The single-job arithmetic is exact. Recomputed by hand and confirmed with `node /tmp/claude-0/audit-lslight/run.mjs` at the page's default costs (32/h x 1.30 = 41.60 loaded, 15% overhead on direct cost, price = cost / (1 - 0.20)): walkway preset 1.4 + 8 x 0.035 + 6 x 0.28 + 0.9 = 4.26 h, 177.22 labor, 252 + 22.40 = 274.40 material, + 55 soft = 506.62, x 1.15 = 582.61, / 0.8 = 728.26; architectural preset 28.55 h (2.03 travel + 10.08 fixtures + 8.10 trench + 3.24 soil + 2.2 transformer + 0.4 + 1.6 + 0.9), 1,187.68 labor, 2,773.40 material (1,332 fixtures + 324 wire + 310 transformer + 432 turf + 85 + 240 + 50.40), cost 4,618.49, price 5,773.11; proposed 650 on the walkway gives profit 67.39 and margin 10.37%. All match the vs-a-flat-150 page. Not a 3 because the 'Same yard, three scopes' comparison (calc.mjs:443-456), which the page FAQ tells the contractor to use 'to see exactly how much of the gap is trench and transformer', prices the fixtures-only row (labelled 'existing transformer ... no trench, no wire run') with the current job's new 300 W transformer invoice (310) and hours (1.8) and the irrigated-turf soil hours (3.24) and sod repair (432) for a trench it does not dig: on the architectural yard it shows fixtures-only 4,799.06 vs new-system 5,773.11 (gap 974), where removing those items gives about 3,431 (gap about 2,342), so the trench-and-transformer share is understated by more than half. A cleared wage field silently becomes 0 (walkway price 473.51 instead of an error).
evidence.completeness: Claimed features run end to end: four fixture types, three scopes, three soils, four transformer sizes, photocell / saw-cut / extra transformer, travel, loaded labor, overhead, margin, walk-away price, per-fixture and effective hourly, hour split, three-scope comparison, proposed-price check, copy bid summary, share link (share.test.mjs), printable proposal with deposit and validity (proposal.test.mjs), opt-out local usage counts (usage.test.mjs). Not built though a page says so: vs-aspire.html:66-67 (and its FAQ JSON-LD) says the tool takes 'transformer sizing, and low-voltage wire gauge and length'; there is no gauge input and the transformer is a price picklist with no sizing. vs-a-flat-150-per-light-special.html:87 says it 'Reports ... the dollar gap against a flat per-light rate'; there is no flat-rate input, only the generic proposed-price check. No TODOs or stubs. Served copy clean (`node platform/pages/served-copy.mjs landscape-lighting-bid-calculator`: no placeholder or retired origin left).
evidence.verification: `cd ventures/landscape-lighting-bid-calculator && node --test '*.test.mjs'`: 138 tests, 138 pass, ~0.32 s. Seven seeded mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: margin /(1-m) -> *(1+m) caught; irrigated turf 2.4 -> 2.0/LF caught; overhead base direct -> labor+material caught; photocell invoice applied unconditionally caught; belowBreakEven < -> <= SURVIVED; 600 W transformer invoice 540 -> 450 SURVIVED; soil hours zeroed for fixtures-only SURVIVED (no test pins the comparison's fixtures-only row values; calc.test.mjs:160-173 only checks ordering). The vs-a-flat page test pins its dollar figures, so the presets it uses are covered; the 600 W kit and boundary cases are not.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (531 lines), the index.html script (readInput, update, kit application), calc.test.mjs, the three marketing pages. Pure functions, frozen presets, validated enums, a strict yes/no flag parser (calc.mjs:117-127) that refuses unknown words, guarded storage, a page test that the share field list matches the form. Defects: number(input.x ?? 0) with Number('') = 0 lets a cleared wage, burden, overhead or margin compute silently (calc.mjs:106-112, 264-267); compareScope overrides scope only and keeps the job's transformer and soil kits even for the fixtures-only row (calc.mjs:444-456), contrary to that row's label; shares.extra and extraCost duplicate extraHardware; proposal.mjs and share.mjs are shared engines copied across bid calculators (share.mjs says so).
evidence.claims: Backed: margin-vs-markup method (README, how-much page), every dollar figure on vs-a-flat-150-per-light-special.html (728.26, 121.38/light, 2,427.53, 4,618.49, 5,773.11, 2,190.96, 3,345.58, recomputed above and pinned by its test), rates labelled 'ballpark crew figures, not a light catalog', disclaimers on all four pages and README naming 'not ... a load calculation, a voltage-drop study', privacy line vs usage.mjs, vs-aspire non-affiliation line and no invented Aspire price. Not backed: index.html:284 (and the FAQ JSON-LD at :11) says 'quoting at or below the walk-away number means the job cannot lose money' - below the walk-away the job loses money, as the tool's own verdict says; vs-aspire.html:66-67 claims transformer sizing and wire gauge inputs that do not exist; vs-a-flat page:87 claims a flat-rate dollar-gap report; index.html:280 FAQ promises the three-scope comparison shows 'exactly how much of the gap is trench and transformer', which the fixtures-only row misstates (see correctness). Hour and material rate cards (calc.mjs:151-241) cite no source; disclosed as ballpark.
evidence.fitness: Job walked through: a lighting contractor bids the architectural preset (6 path, 8 up, 4 well, 2 hardscape, 180 LF irrigated trench, new 300 W, saw-cut) and a homeowner pushing a 150-a-light special. They get a defensible labor/material/overhead/margin build-up, a walk-away price, and a printable proposal in minutes. In the first hour they hit: no transformer load check (60 uplights on a 150 W transformer prices 8,711.58 with no warning, about 420 W on a 120 W usable rating); no wire gauge, so wire is one $/LF regardless of whether the run needs 12, 10 or 8 AWG; wire length equals trench length (no hub or multiple home runs longer than the trench); the comparison table misprices the fixtures-only case they would show the homeowner; a cleared field becomes zero. A contractor who does their own load and voltage-drop design elsewhere and types their own rates gets a sound margin check.
evidence.domain: Compared with standard contractor pricing practice the money method is right: loaded labor, overhead on direct cost, margin on selling price (20% margin = 25% markup). Compared with low-voltage lighting design practice (manufacturer design guides, e.g. the common rules of loading a magnetic transformer to about 80% of its VA rating and keeping fixture voltage within roughly 10.5-12 V; NEC Article 411 for low-voltage lighting systems; NEC Chapter 9 Table 8 copper resistance 12 AWG 1.98, 10 AWG 1.24, 8 AWG 0.778 ohm/kft at 75 C, cited from own knowledge, not fetched), the tool models none of the electrical side: no connected-load total, no 80% transformer check, no VA vs W, no voltage-drop or gauge choice, no multi-tap (12-15 V) transformers, no hub / T vs daisy-chain layout. Hand check on the architectural preset with assumed LED wattages (path 4, up 7, well 8, hardscape 3 = 118 W, 9.83 A at 12 V): one 180 ft home run with all load at the end drops 7.01 V on 12 AWG, 4.39 V on 10 AWG, 2.75 V on 8 AWG (2 x 180 x ohms/ft x 9.83 A), so the job needs a hub layout, heavier wire or higher taps that change the wire $/LF the tool prices flat at 1.80. These gaps are disclosed in README Limitations and page footers ('not an electrical design, a load calculation, a voltage-drop study'), which keeps this at 2 rather than 1.

defects.what: The 'Same yard, three scopes' comparison prices the fixtures-only row (labelled 'existing transformer', described as 'no trench, no wire run') with the current job's new transformer invoice and hours and the soil hours and sod repair for the trench length, because compareScope spreads the job's soil and transformer kits into every row. On the architectural preset it shows fixtures-only 4,799.06 vs new-system 5,773.11 (gap 974) where the fixtures-only job is about 3,431 (gap about 2,342). The FAQ tells the contractor to use this table to see how much of a 150-a-light gap is trench and transformer; it understates that by more than half.

FAQ says 'quoting at or below the walk-away number means the job cannot lose money, but it also cannot pay you'. Below the walk-away price the job loses money (the tool's own verdict says 'loses $X'). The wrong sentence is also in the FAQPage JSON-LD that search engines show.

vs-aspire page (body and FAQ JSON-LD) says the calculator takes 'transformer sizing, and low-voltage wire gauge and length'. There is no wire gauge input and no transformer sizing; the transformer is a price picklist and the README disclaims load and voltage-drop work.

No electrical side at all: no connected-load total, no ~80% transformer loading check (60 uplights on a 150 W transformer prices silently), no voltage drop by gauge and distance (180 ft at 9.8 A drops 7.0 V on 12 AWG), no multi-tap transformers, no hub vs daisy-chain, wire priced at one $/LF and one LF per trench LF. Disclosed as out of scope, but these drive the wire and transformer lines the tool prices.

Hour and material rate cards (fixture hours and prices, wire 1.80/LF, transformer invoices, turf 2.40/LF) cite no source, yet the published vs-a-flat page dollar figures are built on them; labelled ballpark.
vs-a-flat-150 page says the calculator 'Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-light rate'; there is no flat-rate input, only the generic proposed-price check.
A cleared wage, burden, overhead or margin field becomes 0 via Number('') and computes silently (blank wage: walkway price 473.51 with zero labor).
Three seeded mutants survive: the break-even boundary (< vs <=), the 600 W transformer invoice, and fixtures-only soil hours; the compareScope test only checks row ordering, not values.

verdict: The pricing arithmetic is right: loaded labor, overhead on direct cost and margin on price recompute exactly on the walkway and architectural presets and a proposed-price check, and every dollar figure on the flat-150 comparison page reproduces; 138 tests pass and 4 of 7 seeded mutants are caught. It misses the bar on correctness and claims. The three-scope comparison, which the FAQ points the contractor to for exactly the 150-a-light argument, charges the fixtures-only row a new transformer and sod repair for a trench it does not dig, understating the trench-and-transformer gap by more than half on the architectural yard. The FAQ says quoting below the walk-away price cannot lose money, and the Aspire page claims transformer sizing and wire-gauge inputs that do not exist. A landscape lighting contractor would also find no load, 80% transformer, voltage-drop, gauge or hub-layout logic, disclosed as out of scope but driving the very wire and transformer lines priced here. Useful as a margin check for a contractor who designs the electrical side elsewhere.
